# Infrastructure in orbit {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Few firms own a satellite. Almost all depend on one. {.scrollable}

Three services carry most of a firm's dependence on space. Read the last column first: each service is supplied by a handful of states or companies.

| Service | The firm uses it for | Who provides it |
|---|---|---|
| **Positioning, navigation, timing** | tracking, shipping, aviation — and **time**: telecoms, grids, trading venues synchronise their clocks to GNSS | **GPS** (US) · **Galileo** (EU) · **BeiDou** (China) · **GLONASS** (Russia) — each run by a state |
| **Connectivity** | ships, aircraft, mines, remote sites, back-up links | geostationary operators · **constellations** of thousands of satellites in low orbit since 2019 |
| **Earth observation** | crop forecasts, claims, site and supply-chain monitoring, due diligence | agencies · commercial imaging firms |

::: {.get}
Sessions 08 and 10: networks become instruments of power. Today's network is **above** the firm.
:::

::: {.muted}
The change is recent: ESA reports that the number of new payloads kept growing exponentially in 2025, driven by more launches, rideshares and commercial constellations.
:::

# The orbital commons {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## The Outer Space Treaty (1967) {.scrollable}

The Treaty is the constitution of the domain — written for two superpowers, not for a market. Read each article through the right-hand column: what it means for a commercial operator or its customers.

| Article | Rule | For the firm |
|---|---|---|
| **II** | no national appropriation | no one owns an orbit — first occupant keeps it |
| **IV** | no **WMD** in orbit | conventional weapons and **ASAT tests are not banned** |
| **VI** | states answer for **non-governmental** activities: authorisation, continuing supervision | every private satellite has a **state behind it** |
| **VII** | launching state liable for damage | debris has a legal owner |
| **IX** | "due regard"; consult before harmful interference | traffic rules without an enforcer |

::: {.muted}
Plus the **ITU**: frequencies and orbital positions coordinated in order of filing — an incentive to file early and large, sometimes for "paper satellites" that never fly. And **national licensing** (launch, spectrum, remote sensing, exports) turns Article VI into a permit the firm must hold.
:::

## Kessler: the physics of a commons {.scrollable}

::: {.step}
Density passes a threshold → collisions → fragments → **more collisions**: a debris belt that grows on its own
:::

- No one can be excluded; every use depletes it for others — a commons in the strict sense, with physics in place of an economy
- The belt can grow **even if no one launches again**
- Low orbit cleans itself slowly as the atmosphere drags debris down — years at a few hundred km, **decades to centuries** above

::: {.warn}
An orbit's quality is set by the **least careful** actor in it. One test raises every operator's risk — and premium.
:::

::: {.muted}
Kessler & Cour-Palais (1978), *Journal of Geophysical Research* 83(A6): 2637–2646
:::

# Astropolitics {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Three readings of the new space race {.scrollable}

Three authors, three answers to the question "what is space?". Each implies a different risk for a firm that depends on it.

| | Space is… | The argument |
|---|---|---|
| **Dolman (2002)** *Astropolitik* | a **territory** | Mackinder in orbit: control low Earth orbit, control access to space — and the Earth. Session 03's anarchy, with orbits as chokepoints |
| **Pekkanen (2019)** *AJIL Unbound* | a **market** | democratisation · commercialisation · militarisation; **~95% of space technology is dual-use**; treaty-making in decline, so national law and contracts govern |
| **Bowen (2020)** *War in Space* | **infrastructure** for power on Earth | orbit as a "cosmic coastline" — a target when power on Earth is contested |

::: {.get}
One constellation can be a broadband business, a military network and a foreign-policy instrument — at once.
:::

::: {.muted}
The readings do not exclude one another: Pekkanen's dual use explains how a commercial firm ends up carrying the strategic stakes Dolman and Bowen describe.
:::

# Counterspace {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Five categories (SWF, 2026) {.scrollable}

What states can do to deceive, disrupt, deny, degrade or destroy space systems. The two right-hand columns matter most to a firm: whether the damage can be undone, and on whom it falls first.

| Category | Reversible? | Hits first |
|---|---|---|
| **Direct-ascent** missile, launched from Earth | no — and it makes debris | the target, then the whole shell |
| **Co-orbital** — a satellite that approaches, inspects or attacks another | depends | the target |
| **Electronic warfare** — jamming, spoofing | yes | **users** on the ground: ships, aircraft, networks |
| **Directed energy** — lasers, microwaves | partly | imaging satellites |
| **Cyber** — satellites, ground stations, terminals | mostly | **customers** |

::: {.muted}
Note the pattern: the reversible threats land on the ground, on users and customers rather than on the satellite itself.
Samson & Brett (Eds., 2026), *Global Counterspace Capabilities* · 13 countries assessed
:::

## Destroyed vs disrupted {.scrollable}

::::: columns

:::: {.column width="50%"}

### Destructive tests from the ground

- United States 1985, 2008
- **China 2007**
- India 2019
- **Russia 2021**
- US pledge not to test, April 2022; UN General Assembly call, December 2022

::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}

### What is used in war

- **KA-SAT**, 24 Feb 2022: a cyberattack on the ground segment disabled modems in Ukraine and across Europe — wind turbines in Germany lost monitoring
- **GNSS jamming**: Finnair suspends Tartu flights, 2024, as satellite-based approaches become unusable

::::

:::::

::: {.warn}
SWF: only **non-destructive** capabilities are used against satellites in current operations. They fall on the **customers**.
:::

::: {.muted}
Destructive tests make headlines and debris; jamming, spoofing and cyberattacks make the **losses**. A firm's risk register should weight the right-hand column more heavily.
:::

# The debris record {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## ESA, *Space Environment Report 2026* {.scrollable}

Read the method before the figures: what is counted, and from which catalogues, decides what the numbers can tell you.

- **Method:** catalogued (US public catalogue, Russian Vimpel, UK RAE tables) + **asserted** objects known to exist by design, in DISCOS; objects too small to track are out of scope
- **End of 2025:** **44,964** objects in Earth orbit · **16,946** payloads · 25,060 in LEO — more debris than operational satellites since the start of the space age
- **Dominant source:** fragmentations **other than collisions** — mostly old rocket stages and batteries; 9.8 non-deliberate a year on average

::: {.get}
**The target — Figure 2.1:** objects in geocentric orbit by object class, since 1957.
:::

::: {.muted}
ESA Space Debris Office, Issue 10.0, 1 May 2026
:::

## Three events to annotate {.scrollable}

Three events stand out on Figure 2.1. Altitude matters: the higher the event, the longer its fragments stay in orbit.

| Date | Event | Altitude |
|---|---|---|
| **11 Jan 2007** | China destroys **Fengyun-1C** — the largest single source of catalogued debris | ~850 km |
| **10 Feb 2009** | **Iridium 33** and **Cosmos 2251** collide — first accidental collision of two intact satellites: Kessler, observed | ~780 km |
| **15 Nov 2021** | Russia destroys **Cosmos 1408** — almost all re-entered within three years | ~470–490 km |

> **Put it to the room:** where will Fengyun's debris show on a chart built from the public catalogue?

::: {.fragment}
Find out in the practice round.
:::

## What the figure does not measure {.scrollable}

::: {.warn}
A 10-cm fragment and a 5-tonne stage each count **once**. What is too small to catalogue does not count at all.
:::

- Better sensors raise the count with **nothing new in orbit**
- Objects, not **risk** — and not who bears it
- A third limit lies in how the public catalogue **dates** debris: you will meet it in the practice round

::: {.muted}
Before an object count goes on a dashboard, ask what it stands for. Here it measures the catalogue as much as the orbit, and says nothing about which operator — or which customer — carries the exposure.
:::

# One operator {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## The new space race is a one-firm race {.scrollable}

- **Starlink**, first launched May 2019 → the **majority** of the world's operating satellites — with a firm, not a superpower, at the top
- **Ukraine, 2022:** a backbone of military and civil communications — and the operator's decisions on coverage became **war policy**; governments moved to contract for the service directly

::::: columns

:::: {.column width="50%"}

### The panopticon

The operator **sees** who connects, and where

::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}

### The chokepoint

The operator can **switch off** a user, a region, a country

::::

:::::

::: {.get}
Farrell & Newman (S08): concentration + a state that can direct the firm. **Article VI** supplies the state.
:::

::: {.muted}
A firm that depends on one operator therefore depends on that operator's licensing state as well.
:::

## States build their own {.scrollable}

Session 03's logic: states that depend on one American firm respond by building their own capacity — and the licensing state draws the line from the other side.

- **IRIS²** — EU secure connectivity, Regulation (EU) 2023/588
- **Qianfan**, **Guowang** — China's constellations
- **Export controls:** ITAR Category XV · EAR "9x515" since 2014 — a US component means US permission to sell to some customers

::: {.warn}
A second operator licensed by the **same state** is not diversification.
:::

::: {.muted}
Diversification in orbit is measured by licensing state, not by brand: the question for a firm is which governments could direct, restrict or switch off every provider it uses.
:::

# What can the firm do? {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Five channels {.scrollable}

The course's five channels, applied to space: each row is a route by which an event in orbit, or a rule about orbit, reaches the P&L.

| Channel | How space risk arrives |
|---|---|
| **Market access** | export controls, spectrum and landing rights — a terminal that cannot be sold or switched on |
| **Inputs** | a service from one operator, or one state's GNSS |
| **Finance and payments** | GNSS-timed trading and payments; insurance capacity and premiums |
| **Assets and people** | ships and aircraft in jammed or spoofed areas: rerouted flights, misreported positions |
| **Data and operations** | attacks on ground segments and terminals (the KA-SAT modems); lost imagery |

::: {.muted}
Most of these routes run through a supplier, not through the firm's own assets: the exposure sits in contracts for connectivity, timing, imagery and insurance, which is where the dashboard and the strategies that follow must look.
:::

## Four lines for the dashboard {.scrollable}

Each line pairs an indicator with a threshold that triggers a named decision — the format your team dashboard should follow.

1. **Dependence** — share of a critical service (connectivity, imagery, timing) from one operator or one state's system · *> 50% → contract a second*
2. **Interference** — official GNSS-interference warnings (aviation authorities publish them) where the firm's ships, aircraft, sites operate
3. **Environment** — destructive tests and fragmentations in the providers' orbital shells; ESA's yearly indicators
4. **Rules** — export-control lists, licences, ITU filings affecting suppliers or markets

::: {.get}
**Which line would your team's firm put on its dashboard — with which threshold?**
:::

## Strategies {.scrollable}

No strategy removes space risk; each moves it at a cost. Read the last column as the question to ask before relying on it.

| Strategy | Cost | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| **Multi-orbit, multi-operator** — geostationary + low orbit, two providers | price, integration | same licensing state? |
| **Multi-constellation receivers** — GPS + Galileo (+ others) | small | one jammer blinds them all locally |
| **Terrestrial back-up** — clocks, fibre, cellular | capital | not at sea, not in remote sites |
| **Insurance** — in-orbit and third-party liability | premium | thin market; capacity leaves after losses |
| **Compliance by design** — classify every space component | staff, delays | rules move with the balance of power |

# The Tableau skill of the day {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## A stock from flows · HHI · an action {.scrollable}

The catalogue records flows — a launch date and, for objects that have re-entered, a decay date. The number in orbit is a stock: launches minus decays, accumulated year by year. Concentration is measured with the HHI, the sum of squared owner shares.

```text
Change      =  IF [Event] = "LAUNCH_DATE" THEN 1 ELSE -1 END     // after pivoting the two dates
In orbit    =  RUNNING_SUM(SUM([Change]))                        // Quick Table Calculation
Owner share =  {FIXED [Launch year], [OWNER] : COUNT([NORAD_CAT_ID])}
             / {FIXED [Launch year] : COUNT([NORAD_CAT_ID])}
```

1. **Running total** by year, `OBJECT_TYPE` → Colour: the target figure
2. **HHI** of who launches, year by year
3. **Action:** click a year → see who launched that year (*Dashboard → Actions → Filter*, `Year` mapped to `Launch year`)

::: {.muted}
The HHI is built so that it adds up correctly over rows; a value near its maximum means one owner launches almost everything.
:::

::: {.check}
Click a year; the owners chart follows. That is the interaction your team dashboard needs.
:::
